claims.statement: Capacity should be enforced before unlimited work enters the runtime: bounding work in system kept the surge out of the runtime, and open admission turned timeouts into retries and an unbounded queue.

article: The Noisy Neighbour Is Your Own Finance Team
§8 Orchestration owns concurrency, queues and backpressure
claims.statement: Multi-tenant agent platforms need tenant-aware resource controls, not only global limits: under one global FIFO the finance run starved support; with weighted fair scheduling and a bulkhead, support was served and the batch still completed, later.

article: The Noisy Neighbour Is Your Own Finance Team
§8 Orchestration owns concurrency, queues and backpressure
claims.statement: Concurrency must be bounded independently of incoming request volume: unbounded concurrency slowed every workflow and spent most of its cost on attempts nobody was waiting for; slots, a bounded queue and deadline-aware dequeue kept goodput up.

article: Unlimited Reasoning Is Not an Architecture
§6 Give every workflow a resource envelope
claims.statement: Production agents need explicit execution budgets, propagated to child workflows: the envelope stopped a runaway loop and bounded a coordinator with sub-agents, where per-agent budgets did not; calibrated on a development sample, it also stopped some legitimate workflows of the blind sample.

article: The Cheapest Model Is Not Always an Eligible One
claims.note: Synthetic eligibility contract and success table: no statement about the quality of any real model.
claims.statement: Model routing should optimise within a declared quality/policy contract, not cost alone: inside the contract, routing cost less per successful workflow than all-large with no violation, deferring explicitly during a throttle; optimising cost alone (all-small, any fallback) left the contract.

article: Context and Tools Have Their Own Limits
§10 Context and knowledge have operational cost
claims.statement: Context and retrieval need resource controls like model execution: bounded retrieval kept every declared required evidence id with far fewer tokens, and a cache keyed by tenant, principal scope and versions hit without leaking or going stale, unlike a query-text cache.

article: Context and Tools Have Their Own Limits
§11 Tools have a different scaling limit
claims.statement: Tool capacity must be governed independently of model capacity: the gateway held the payments API inside its capacity with no 503s and far fewer attempts; alone on a FIFO queue it moved the wait into the runtime's slots, and composed with fair scheduling it served support too.

Behaviourally relevant non-code changes must create a distinguishable agent release: six single-artifact changes produced six new release ids under one unchanged image digest, and every telemetry row is attributable to its release. (The behaviour a tool description causes is declared in the scripted agent.)
Behavioural releases should pass machine-checkable gates before receiving production traffic: three candidates with good averages and one broken invariant each were blocked and granted no traffic.

Agent releases require behavioural canaries and rollback on operational evidence, not process health: a release that passed the offline gate and kept its error rate rolled back on tool-call amplification; a clean one was promoted; a raw-average comparison would have rolled the clean one back; the rollback did not undo replies already sent.

article: We Built the Overload on Purpose
claims.statement: The proof can fail: with the admission bound removed, the E1 invariant check breaks.

rests_on: OPS-E1 and OPS-E7 as illustrations, not tests of autoscaling
claims.statement: Autoscaling helps but does not remove provider quotas, downstream limits, budgets or tenant fairness; a queue absorbs imbalance, it does not create capacity.

rests_on: OPS-E10-C06 shows only the side-effect half
claims.statement: Rollback across a stateful agent platform is harder than rolling back a stateless binary: indexes, memory, migrations and external side effects need compatible versions or reconciliation.

article: What This POC Does Not Prove
claims.statement: Real provider latency, quotas and prices; real model quality; human approval capacity; shadow traffic; real tool limits. Every number in this POC is a simulation unit.

contract: Production AI Engineering Proof Contract v1

experiments.claim: Capacity should be enforced before unlimited work enters the runtime.
experiments.invariant: work in system <= slots + queue bound
limitations: Simulated clients and providers; the bound protects the runtime, it does not create capacity: refused requests are the cost
experiments.question: When offered demand exceeds capacity, does bounding work in system keep the overload out of the runtime?
experiments.setup: Black Friday surge: support requests at a multiple of capacity for 120 s, then the evening; same clients in both arms (they give up after 20 s and retry)
experiments.title: Admission before execution
experiments.variable: admission: open (unbounded queue) vs bounded work in system with a capacity error and Retry-After

experiments.claim: Multi-tenant agent platforms need tenant-aware resource controls, not only global limits.
experiments.invariant: finance never holds more than its bulkhead
limitations: Two tenants and one shared resource (slots); real platforms share more (providers, tools, caches)
experiments.question: When one tenant floods the shared platform, do global limits alone protect the other tenant?
experiments.setup: support at a steady rate; finance submits its reconciliation run in ten seconds; same 32 slots
experiments.title: Tenant fairness: the noisy neighbour is your own finance team
experiments.variable: scheduling: one global FIFO vs weighted fair scheduling with a finance bulkhead

experiments.claim: Concurrency must be bounded independently of incoming request volume.
experiments.invariant: running attempts <= slots at every event; no attempt starts after its client's deadline
limitations: Contention is a declared processor-sharing model, not a measured runtime
experiments.question: Does bounding concurrency, independently of demand, protect the work the runtime does?
experiments.setup: overload at 1.5x capacity for 60 s, then light load; same clients
experiments.title: Bounded concurrency, backpressure and deadlines
experiments.variable: unbounded concurrency vs slots + bounded queue + deadline-aware dequeue + cancellation

experiments.claim: Production agents need explicit execution budgets, propagated to child workflows.
experiments.invariant: the runaway stops on its envelope; the coordinator's total stays within its envelope
limitations: The envelope is calibrated on a 350-workflow development sample (max x 1.25); a larger sample or explicit retry allowance would cut fewer legitimate workflows
experiments.question: Does an explicit envelope stop runaway execution, including across sub-agents, and what does it cut?
experiments.setup: a refund whose payment never settles; a coordinator with three sub-agents, one stuck, re-delegated; 350 calibrated normal workflows
experiments.title: Workflow resource envelopes, propagated to children
experiments.variable: budgets: none vs per-agent vs a propagated envelope

experiments.claim: Model routing should optimise within a quality/policy boundary, not optimise cost alone.
experiments.invariant: routed never uses an ineligible profile
limitations: The success table is declared, not measured: this tests routing within the contract, not any model's quality
A validator that catches every wrong answer is assumed; uncaught wrong answers would cost more than their tokens
experiments.question: Can routing reduce modelled cost without leaving a declared capability and data-policy contract, including during a provider throttle?
experiments.setup: 800 workflows (support mix + finance), the EU private deployment throttled for 30 s
experiments.title: Routing inside an eligibility contract
experiments.variable: all-large vs all-small vs routed vs routed with any fallback

experiments.claim: Context and retrieval need resource controls just like model execution.
experiments.invariant: the scoped cache never serves across principals or versions
limitations: Relevance scores are a frozen fixture, not a retriever; required ids make the check mechanical, not a measure of retrieval quality
experiments.question: Can retrieval be bounded without losing the evidence a query needs, and can a cache help without leaking or going stale?
experiments.setup: 12 fixture queries with declared required evidence ids; a 24-lookup cache sequence with a knowledge and a policy version change
experiments.title: Context budgets and cache scope
experiments.variable: naive vs bounded retrieval; query-text vs scoped cache key

experiments.claim: Tool capacity must be governed independently of model capacity.
experiments.invariant: with the gateway, calls in flight <= the API's capacity and no 503
limitations: Read-only tool: idempotency of writes (R2) is not exercised
experiments.question: Does governing a tool's capacity independently of the runtime protect the downstream, and what else does it need?
experiments.setup: payments-status API (capacity 8, connection limit 16, 20 rps) behind a 64-slot runtime; a finance run and support traffic
experiments.title: A tool gateway in front of a constrained downstream
experiments.variable: direct calls with immediate retries vs the gateway vs the gateway composed with fair scheduling

experiments.claim: Behaviourally relevant non-code changes must create a distinguishable agent release.
experiments.invariant: one image digest; seven release ids; one artifact per diff; every row attributable
limitations: The behaviour a change causes is declared in the scripted agent: the size of R42-a's effect is a modelling assumption, not a measurement; what is tested is release identity, attribution, and (E9, E10) whether gates and canaries notice
experiments.question: If no code changes, does the platform still see a new release?
experiments.setup: R41 and six candidates, each changing one artifact; the same 300-workflow Cyber Monday sample replayed under each
experiments.title: The behavioural release

experiments.claim: Behavioural releases should pass machine-checkable gates before receiving production traffic.
experiments.invariant: a blocked candidate gets no traffic
limitations: Task success comes from the declared outcome model; tool-call volume is not a gate criterion (an operational property, left to the canary)
experiments.question: Do machine-checkable gates stop a release whose averages look fine but which breaks an invariant?
experiments.setup: a 40-case offline suite (historical, adversarial, synthetic) under R41 and five candidates
experiments.title: Offline evals and invariant gates

experiments.claim: Agent releases require behavioural canaries and rollback based on operational evidence, not merely process health.
experiments.invariant: after a rollback, no request reaches the candidate
limitations: Canary effects are simulated replies; write-capable canaries need scoped or sandboxed execution or reconciliation (R2)
experiments.question: Does a canary that watches behaviour, not status codes, catch a release the offline gate passed, and leave a clean one alone?
experiments.setup: Cyber Monday support traffic; 10 / 50 / 100 % stages; windows of 60 candidate workflows; frozen guardrails
experiments.title: A behavioural canary, promotion and rollback
experiments.variable: the candidate (R42-a, R42-e) and the comparison (mix-adjusted, raw)

experiments.claim: The E1 invariant check detects a missing admission bound.
experiments.invariant: work in system <= slots + queue bound (expected to break)
experiments.question: Can the proof fail? Remove the admission bound and the E1 invariant must break.
experiments.setup: E1's controlled arm, identical except that the admission bound is removed
experiments.title: Negative control: admission removed

items.text: Admission with a work-in-system bound and an explicit capacity error (128 = slots + queue bound)
Weighted fair scheduling (deficit round robin, 3:1) with a finance bulkhead of 16
Bounded concurrency, deadline-aware dequeue and cooperative cancellation
Workflow resource envelopes and a ledger shared with child workflows
Routing inside an eligibility contract with policy-aware fallback
Bounded retrieval and a cache keyed by tenant, principal scope, knowledge and policy version
A tool gateway: per-tool concurrency, rate limit, bounded priority wait, circuit breaker
Content-addressed release manifests, a registry that refuses ungated releases, an invariant gate and a mix-adjusted canary

classes.meaning: the actual mechanism was exercised: each control is real code, executed on every simulated request

items.text: The clock (integer simulated milliseconds), the model providers (latency, quotas, 429), the downstream APIs (capacity, 503, 429) and the clients (timeouts, retries)
Scripted agents: the plans are fixed per workflow type; the only behaviour a release changes is declared (a tool description, a prompt length, a routing table)
Cost in cost units (cu): synthetic per-1k-token rates, per-query and per-call charges; not any provider's prices
The eligibility contract and the success table by capability gap (config/models.toml): routing is tested within them, never real model quality
Processor-sharing contention beyond 32 concurrent workflows; a downstream that slows above its capacity and refuses at its connection limit
A validator that catches every wrong answer; a person handling an escalation costs 60 cu

classes.meaning: declared: an assumption the simulation encodes and the article states

items.text: Workload: seeded arrivals, cases and long-tail shapes (seed 4917; E4 calibration seed 1101)
The knowledge fixture (120 documents, 12 queries with declared required evidence ids, a 24-lookup cache sequence) and the 40-case offline eval suite (scripts/make_fixtures.py)

classes.meaning: synthetic inputs generated deterministically and frozen

items.text: A Black Friday surge at 20 requests/s; a finance run of 3,000 items in ten seconds
A payment that never settles (a runaway loop) and a coordinator that re-delegates a failing sub-agent
A 30 s throttle of the EU private deployment
Candidate releases: one tool description, one prompt, one retrieval top-k, one knowledge index, one policy, one routing table; three that break an invariant
The admission bound removed (the negative control)
